AbstractText.Label: BACKGROUND
AbstractText.content: After its initial use, resistance to difenacoum has been detected rapidly in rats in north-east Hampshire and north-west Berkshire in England. Resistance to difenacoum has been reported to be stronger in rats from Berkshire than rats from Hampshire. Surprisingly, after the discovery of the Vkorc1 gene, rats from Berkshire and Hampshire were all shown to be homozygous for the L120Q mutation in the Vkorc1.

AbstractText.Label: RESULTS
AbstractText.content: This study aims to evaluate the resistance of Berkshire rats to confirm their extreme resistance and determine mechanisms supporting this resistance. For this, we created a quasicongenic rat F7 strain by using Berkshire rat as a donor to introduce the L120Q mutation in the Vkorc1 into the genetic background of an anticoagulant susceptible recipient strain. The use of F7 rats enabled to demonstrate i/ the level of resistance to difenacoum conferred by the L120Q mutation, , ii/the codominance of L120 and Q120 alleles, iii/ the extreme resistance of Berkshire rats compared to Q120/Q120 rats due to additional resistance mechanisms, and iv/ certainly the involvement of CYP450 enzymes in this extreme resistance.

AbstractText.Label: CONCLUSION
AbstractText.content: This study demonstrated that an elevated CYP450-oxidative metabolism leading to an accelerated difenacoum detoxification is involved in the Berkshire phenotype.
